author: Shakespeare
title: Ariel’s song
where: *The Tempest*, Act 1, Scene 2, with Act 3, Scene 2 and the Epilogue
about: Ferdinand, a young prince, has come ashore alone from a shipwreck and believes his father, the king, has drowned. Ariel, a spirit he cannot see, sings this to him. His father is alive, on another part of the island, and Ariel knows it. The second passage is spoken by Caliban, a slave, when Ariel’s unseen music frightens the butler and the jester he is leading to kill his master, Prospero, the magician who rules the island. The third is Prospero’s own, spoken to the audience when the play is over.

view.says: Auden wrote that this song is a dirge in form only. The feelings of a mourning son are no part of it. It is a spell, and what it does is change Ferdinand’s attitude to his grief, from rebellion to awe and acceptance. The loss is not made less. The song lets him accept that his father belongs to the past, and then his future is in front of him: Miranda.
view.quote: It is a magic spell, the effect of which is, not to lessen his feeling of loss, but to change his attitude towards his grief
view.source: “Music in Shakespeare,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 525–26

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: seven syllables and four beats, the line beginning on a beat
lenses.caption: From its second line to its seventh the song keeps one measure: seven syllables, four beats, the line beginning on a beat. Oberon and Puck say their charms in this measure in A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and so do the witches in Macbeth. Auden called this song a magic spell, and this is the measure of those spells. The rule under each line is the measure and the dots are the speaking voice. They part most in the fourth and fifth lines, which say what is happening to the body. At sea-change two stresses fall together, which slows the voice on a word that was new. In the next line, Into something rich and strange, voice and measure agree again.
lenses.why: The song is in the measure of the charms in A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Macbeth, and Auden calls it a spell; the voice leaves the measure most where two stresses slow it on the new word.

points.say: The first line has eight syllables and begins off the beat. Three of its first four syllables are stressed.
The last line has eight syllables too. It ends on three stresses in a row. The first two are the sound of the bell: *ding-dong* is a word made from it.

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The charms in this measure: *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*, Act 2, Scene 2 and Act 3, Scene 2; *Macbeth*, Act 1, Scene 3 and Act 4, Scene 1. Auden calls the song a spell in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 525. Stresses that fall together: Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 5. *Sea-change* as a new word: *A New English Dictionary*, under Sea.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: The first four lines rhyme by turns: lies with eyes, made with fade. Each rhyme waits a line for its partner. From sea-change on the song rhymes in pairs, and strange answers change at once. A rhyme that comes back at once makes its two lines one unit, a couplet. This one holds the words Auden gave his class in 1941 as the central theme of the sea scenes in Pericles and The Tempest. Sounds come back inside the lines as well: f four times in the first line, and s four times across the couplet.
lenses.why: The rhyme changes from alternate lines to couplets at the sentence about the sea-change, so those two lines are heard as one unit; Auden took their words as the theme of the sea scenes in Pericles and The Tempest.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. That a rhyme which returns at once makes its two lines one unit: Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 4, on the short couplet. What Auden told his class about these words: Donald Pearce’s notes of the lecture, p. 149.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: chiasmus
lenses.plain: a crossing: two things are named, then named again in the opposite order
lenses.caption: Two lines say one thing in opposite order. The first goes from the body to the sea: bones, then coral. The second goes from the sea to the body: pearls, then eyes. Neither line says like. The verbs are plain ones, are and were: coral is made of his bones, and what are pearls now were his eyes. Auden told his class that the theme named in this song is transformation, almost transmutation in the alchemist’s sense, one substance changed into another. These two lines state such a change as fact, twice.
lenses.why: The two lines name body and sea in crossed order and join them with the plain verbs are and were, never with like; Auden said the theme the song names is transformation, close to an alchemist’s transmutation.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the two lines themselves. Auden on transformation: Donald Pearce’s notes of the lecture, p. 149. What transmutation means: the Online Etymology Dictionary.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: Old English *fæthm* was the length of the outstretched arms, and also an embrace.
The lexicon of Shakespeare’s words puts this line under the sense: to be perishable.
The same lexicon puts this line under the sense: to undergo or experience, in a good or a bad sense.
The first edition of the Oxford dictionary gives this song as its only example of the word.

notes.gloss: the sound of a funeral bell

lenses.caption: The Oxford dictionary’s earliest example of sea-change is this song, and Shakespeare appears to have made the word for this line. Suffer here means undergo, and fade means perish. So the sentence says that every part of him that could perish is changed by the sea instead. Strange could mean foreign or new as well as wonderful. Fathom is six feet, at first the length of two outstretched arms. Knell is the sound of a bell rung at a funeral. The words are those of a dirge, and Auden’s point is that the song is a dirge in form only.
lenses.why: The sentence turns on a word first recorded here, sea-change, and on suffer in its sense of undergo: the text says the body is changed and does not perish, which is the transformation Auden names.
lenses.stands: *A New English Dictionary*, under Sea, for the first record of *sea-change*. Alexander Schmidt’s *Shakespeare-Lexicon* for *suffer*, *fade*, *strange*, *fathom* and *knell*; its entries for *fade* and *suffer* quote this line. The Online Etymology Dictionary for the fathom as two arms’ length. The lines themselves. Auden on the dirge: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 525.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: A tavern band is called a *noise* in *Henry IV, Part 2*.
In Act 1 Ferdinand uses the word of Ariel’s first song.
The lexicon puts this line under the sense: it seemed to me in sleep, I dreamt.
The verb can mean to weep, but the lexicon puts this line under the sense: to cry for something, to demand it eagerly.

lenses.caption: Noises is Caliban’s first word for what Ariel has just played, unseen, on a pipe and a tabor, a small drum. The lexicon of Shakespeare’s words puts this line under the sense music; a band of musicians was called a noise. Then come sounds and sweet airs: an air is a piece of music, played or sung. He speaks of instruments and voices and of no player, and he never says Ariel’s name in the play. In Act 4 Ariel reports that with his tabor he charmed the ears of Caliban and his two companions. Auden wrote that without Prospero Ariel can be known to Caliban only as these sounds and sweet airs.
lenses.why: Caliban’s words name what is heard, music and airs, instruments and voices, and no player; Auden says that without Prospero Ariel can be known to Caliban only as these sounds and sweet airs.
lenses.stands: The stage directions for [Ariel’s entry](#/read/tempest/a3s2:36) and for [the tabor and pipe](#/read/tempest/a3s2:111). Alexander Schmidt’s *Shakespeare-Lexicon* under Noise and Air, which cite these lines, and under Tabor. A count of who speaks Ariel’s name in the text printed here. Ariel’s [report in Act 4](#/read/tempest/a4s1:97). Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 131.

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.caption: The last seven lines are one sentence. And sometimes, and then and that, when join waking to sleep, sleep to the dream, and the dream to waking. The lexicon of Shakespeare’s words puts will hum and would open under use and custom, what happens again and again, and will make is the same will. The sentence’s other verbs are past: methought, cried. No verb in this speech is a future, though earlier in the scene Caliban plots in the future tense. Auden took Caliban to stand for the natural, which keeps to what is necessary and cannot imagine possibility; a vague dream, he wrote, is the nearest it comes. Stephano answers in the future: will prove, shall have.
lenses.why: One sentence joins waking, sleep, dream and waking, and its verbs tell custom and the past, with no future among them; Auden says the natural cannot imagine possibility and comes nearest to it in a vague dream.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The Folio of 1623 and the Cambridge edition of 1863, which both run the last seven lines as one sentence. Alexander Schmidt’s *Shakespeare-Lexicon* under Will, for the *will* and *would* of custom. The lines themselves, Stephano’s reply, and Caliban’s plot [earlier in the scene](#/read/tempest/a3s2:54). Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 131–32.

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: ten syllables and five beats, the line beginning off the beat, without rhyme

127.7.voice: /x x / x/ x | x x x /

lenses.caption: Five of the nine lines run a syllable past the last beat: noises, hurt not, voices, dreaming, riches. A handbook of verse counts such extra syllables among the freedoms of Shakespeare’s late verse, and says the placing of a pause can fit verse to meaning. The long sentence pauses three times after a third beat, at ears, at sleep again and at upon me, and each time goes on in the same line. So sleep, the dream and the waking each begin in mid-line.
lenses.why: The pauses of the long sentence fall inside the line, so sleep, the dream and the waking each begin in mid-line; five lines run a syllable past the measure, a freedom a handbook finds in Shakespeare’s late verse.

points.say: Two stresses fall together, which slows the voice. The same happens at *long sleep*, in the fifth line.
This is the first of three pauses, each after a third beat.
The speech stops on a line of three beats. Three earlier lines paused after their third beat and went on.
This text prints the reply as prose, so no measure is drawn under it.

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 4, on Shakespeare’s late blank verse and on the extra syllable at the end of a line, and chapter 5, on the pause and on stresses that fall together.

lenses.label: Scene
lenses.what: who speaks verse and who speaks prose in Act 3, Scene 2
lenses.caption: As this text prints it, the scene has 66 speeches. Stephano, a butler, and Trinculo, a jester, speak 42, all in prose; two lines are sung. Caliban speaks 20: the first five are prose and the other fifteen verse, 54 lines. Ariel, unseen, has the other four, each a few words. Shakespeare sometimes gives prose to characters of low rank and verse to those above them. Here the two servants keep to prose, and the slave, whom they call monster seventeen times, speaks verse, as Prospero, Miranda and Ferdinand do in every speech they have. Auden wrote that Caliban, his savage innocence lost, is open to further corruption by the vices of civilization that these two bring.
lenses.why: Shakespeare gives the butler and the jester prose and gives the slave they call monster the verse of Prospero and the lovers; Auden says the two men bring civilized vices to a Caliban who has lost his savage innocence.
lenses.stands: Counts in the text printed here: the speeches of [Act 3, Scene 2](#/read/tempest/a3s2), a speech being one turn under a speaker’s name, with verse and prose as that text prints them; the word *monster*, compounds included; and every speech of Prospero, Miranda and Ferdinand. The play’s list of persons. On prose and rank: the Royal Shakespeare Company’s and Shakespeare’s Globe’s pages on his language. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 130.

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: four beats in seven or eight syllables, rhymed in pairs
lenses.caption: Four beats, seven or eight syllables, and rhyme: this is the measure of Ariel’s song, the first passage here. Shakespeare gives it to charms, and Puck closes A Midsummer Night’s Dream in it, asking for pardon and for the clapping of hands, as Prospero does. Prospero speaks it for the first time here, as he says his charms are overthrown. In the third line the sentence stops at most faint. A handbook of verse says a strong pause inside so short a line can break its rhythm. Auden taught in 1941 that the play deals with an old theme, the giving up of more than ordinary powers.
lenses.why: Prospero first speaks the measure of Shakespeare’s charms, and of Puck’s last speech, as he says his own charms are overthrown, and it stops in mid-line at most faint; Auden’s theme for the play is such powers given up.

points.say: Voice and measure agree on every syllable.
Stress meets stress across the full stop.
A second full stop inside a line. Here the beat is kept.
Lines 11 to 18 of the Epilogue are left out before this line.

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The charms in this measure: *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*, Act 2, Scene 2, and *Macbeth*, Act 4, Scene 1; Puck’s last speech ends the *Dream*. A count of Prospero’s verse in the text printed here. Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 4, on the pause inside a short couplet. Auden’s theme for the play: Donald Pearce’s notes, p. 150.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: The lines rhyme in pairs. A rhyme that returns at once makes each pair one unit, a couplet, and in so short a line the sense usually pauses with the line. Prospero’s first two sentences stop in mid-line, in the third line and the fifth. In the twelve lines shown a sentence ends with its couplet twice, at hands and at free, and both sentences ask the audience to release him. At the first of these the rhyme words differ by one letter: the bands hold him, and the hands can free him.
lenses.why: In the lines shown a sentence closes with its couplet, the unit the rhyme makes, only at hands and at free, the two places where Prospero asks the audience to release him; the other two stop inside a line.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 4, on the short couplet.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: As Act 5 opens Prospero says that his charms do not crack. The word comes through French from Latin *carmen*, a song, a verse, an enchantment.
In Act 5 Ariel reports the king and his followers confined together, all prisoners, who cannot move till Prospero releases them.
In Act 5 Prospero tells the court they are spell-stopped, and has Ariel untie the spell on Caliban and the two men.
The lexicon sets this line beside Puck’s request at the close of *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*, which it explains as clap hands, applaud.
The lexicon gives leniency first, and quotes these two lines under the church’s sense.

lenses.caption: In Act 5 four of these words are Prospero’s to use on others: the king’s party is confin’d until his order to release it, he has a spell untied, and his last words to Ariel set him free. In the Epilogue each is turned on Prospero: confin’d by you, your spell, release me, set me free. Auden wrote that Prospero forgives with contempt, as a man whose enemies are entirely in his power. Here the power is the audience’s, and he asks their indulgence. The lexicon of Shakespeare’s words puts this line under the word’s sense in the Roman Catholic church: absolution from censure and punishment.
lenses.why: Confined, spell, release and free are words of Prospero’s power in Act 5; in the Epilogue each is turned on him, and the man whose pardon Auden calls contemptuous asks his hearers for indulgence.
lenses.stands: Act 5 in the text printed here: [the king’s party confined](#/read/tempest/a5s1:9), [the order to release it](#/read/tempest/a5s1:15), [the spell untied](#/read/tempest/a5s1:133) and [Prospero’s last words to Ariel](#/read/tempest/a5s1:188). The lines themselves. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 129. Alexander Schmidt’s *Shakespeare-Lexicon* under Indulgence.

lenses.label: Pardon

ties.say: Both begin with *As you*: what the hearer hopes for comes first.
To Caliban the pardon is Prospero’s to give. In the Epilogue it is the pardon his hearers hope for themselves.
Then what the hearer is to do. Caliban is to make Prospero’s cell neat. The audience is asked to set Prospero free.

lenses.caption: Set against the last two lines are Prospero’s words to Caliban near the end of Act 5. Auden found in these words Prospero’s attitude to all the enemies he pardons, and wrote that the thought that he too may have done wrong and need forgiving never comes to him. The two sentences are built alike: as you hope for pardon, then what the hearer is to do. To Caliban the pardon is my pardon. In the Epilogue the hearers are the ones who would pardon’d be, for their own crimes, and Prospero asks their indulgence for himself.
lenses.why: The Epilogue’s last couplet is built like the words to Caliban in which Auden finds Prospero’s attitude to all those he pardons; there the pardon is his to give, and here he asks his hearers for indulgence.
lenses.stands: The two passages as they stand together on the page. Prospero’s [words to Caliban](#/read/tempest/a5s1:171) in Act 5, with Alexander Schmidt’s *Shakespeare-Lexicon* under Trim and Handsomely. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 129.

auden.says: Donald Pearce, who took the class, wrote down what he could after the lectures. According to his notes, Auden said in December 1941 that the sea in Shakespeare is always where new life comes from, where the old is laid down and treasure is found. What this song says is the central theme of the sea scenes in *Pericles* and *The Tempest*. The change comes close to transmutation, as an alchemist would mean the word, and it works on people too, on their minds and their lives, not only on things.
auden.quote: What Shakespeare is dealing with here is transformation
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 134 and 148–49

auden.says: Of Ariel’s voice Auden wrote that it should be as little personal and as much like an instrument as a voice can be, because Ariel has no human feelings to express. The songs sung to the Duke in *Twelfth Night* and to Mariana in *Measure for Measure*, he wrote, do not change their hearers, and only settle each more firmly in a mood already there. The effect of Ariel’s two songs on Ferdinand is more like that of the instrumental music a physician orders for the unconscious Thaisa in *Pericles*.
auden.source: “Music in Shakespeare,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 508 and 525

auden.says: In Pearce’s notes of the December lecture Auden called the play a fairy tale: a hero who has erred comes home from a land of marvels to rule again. Prospero’s error was to neglect his dukedom out of an egotistical wish to perfect himself in secret arts. The theme is an old one, the giving up of more than ordinary powers for the blessings of ordinary life, as Faust gives them up. What Prospero learns on the island is the art of life, though he learns magic too. Caliban is what is beastly in human nature: it has to be held in its place and cannot be removed or ignored.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 150–51

auden.says: In *The Dyer’s Hand* Auden takes Caliban to stand for the natural and Ariel for the spirit of imagination, ideally an unseen voice. Shakespeare, he says, has written the part so that Caliban, brutal and corrupt as he is, has the better of his argument with Prospero, who is largely to blame for his corruption. Prospero and Ariel are bound by a contract, and Ariel is released when the play ends.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 129–34

auden.says: Auden called the play a disquieting work. The guilty repent and the injured pardon, he wrote, more in form than in fact, and only Alonso seems truly sorry. Prospero is to be admired for his gifts and for his strength, and cannot be liked. In “Music in Shakespeare” Auden adds that the play ends more sourly than the three comedies before it, and that the victory of justice seems to Prospero a duty more than a joy.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass” and “Music in Shakespeare,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 128–29 and 526–27

auden.says: Auden judged the play manichean, because it blames nature for the conflict of nature and spirit and makes spirit innocent. He set *The Magic Flute* against it, as too optimistic where this play is too pessimistic. In the opera Papageno, who stands for the natural, gets his Papagena as a reward, and their duet shows, humbly and innocently, the attitude that Caliban shows, guilty and defiant, when Prospero charges him with trying to rape Miranda.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 130 and 134

auden.says: In “Music in Shakespeare” Auden says that Shakespeare uses instrumental music in two ways: on social occasions, and, unexpectedly, as an image in sound of a world of magic or of the supernatural. Spirits such as Oberon and Ariel may command such music, and so may a wise man such as Prospero, to work magically on human beings. Solemn music mostly comes from off stage, where no one sees who plays it, so that those on stage cannot choose how to answer it: either they do not hear it or it does to them what they cannot control.
auden.source: “Music in Shakespeare,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 507–8

sources: The text: William Shakespeare, *The Tempest*, as Project Gutenberg prints it (no. 1540).
W. H. Auden, *The Dyer’s Hand and Other Essays* (1962): “Balaam and His Ass,” pp. 128–34; “Music in Shakespeare,” pp. 507–8 and 525–27.
Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 134 and 148–51: notes made after Auden’s lectures in the fall of 1941.
*A New English Dictionary on Historical Principles* (the first edition of the Oxford English Dictionary), vol. VIII, part 2, under Sea (first published in 1911): the first record of *sea-change*.

Alexander Schmidt, *Shakespeare-Lexicon* (Berlin, 1902), at the Perseus Digital Library: Fade, Suffer, Strange, Knell, Fathom and Ding-dong; Afeard, Noise, Air, Tabor, Twangling, Methought, That, Cry and Will; Charm, Confine, Spell, Release, Band, Hand, Crime, Indulgence, Free, Trim and Handsomely.

Shakespeare’s other plays: *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*, Act 2, Scene 2 and Act 3, Scene 2 (the charms of Oberon and Puck) and Act 5, Scene 1 (Puck’s last speech); *Macbeth*, Act 1, Scene 3 and Act 4, Scene 1 (the witches); [*Henry IV, Part 2*, Act 2, Scene 4](#/read/henry-iv-2/a2s4:7), for a band called a noise.

caveats: What Auden said in class in 1941 is known from notes that a student, Donald Pearce, wrote down after the lectures. It is not Auden’s own text.
The stresses marked are one reader’s hearing of the lines. Another reader could fairly mark a few syllables otherwise.

Editions do not print Act 3, Scene 2 alike. The counts of verse and prose follow the text printed here. The Folio of 1623 sets two of Caliban’s first five speeches as verse, and sets several speeches of Stephano and Trinculo, the reply shown here among them, as short lines.
The two full stops inside Caliban’s speech are an editor’s. The Folio has a comma and a colon there, and no full stop before the end of the speech.
The third passage leaves out lines 11 to 18 of the Epilogue. In those lines a third sentence ends with its couplet.
